title: I watched both "Miracle on 34th Street" and "It's A Wonderful Life" each for the first time and they couldn't be more different. (I had an idea of the plot of "Miracle", but I had absolutely no idea what "Wonderful Life" was about, other than its mawkish reputation.)

commenti.body: Glad you elected to watch the B&W It's a Wonderful Life rather than the Ted Turner abomination. The Greatest Gift novella that inspired the movie was itself loosely based on A Christmas Carol, so that's where the hypothetical timeline conceit came from. And I think you're right - despite its reputation, it's barely a Christmas movie. I've always found it to be more of a quarter-life crisis film with a Christmas bow on it. One of my absolute favourites.

I would be curious to hear your opinion on which Miracle on  34th Street you like better. I've never seen the original. Only the remake from 94 and I watch it every Christmas. 

I completely get wanting to watch It’s a wonderful life in its original black and white. I only had the option to watch the colored version when I first saw the movie and had to turn off the colors on my TV because I really wanted to stick with the original experience. I was a little disappointed because from my limited knowledge beforehand, I assumed that the movie was actually about his meeting with Clarence in its entirety (or at least a little longer). Not the last 30 minutes only. I still liked it fine, but I don’t get the same joy out of it that must people presumably do.

Scrooge from 1951 with Alastair Sim is also incredible - really gothic adaptation that treats it like the ghost story it is, and Sim gives the best performance of Scrooge imo. I always try to watch it late at night on Christmas Eve.

Probably should rewatch A Christmas Story since it's been forever. Christmas Vacation is a yearly watch. Lots of big laughs!

The holidays have a peak in suicides for a reason. Lots of people feel lonely and unloved  and that their lives had no meaning or purpose beyond themselves, if they even have a personal meaning or purpose. That even George, a hometown hero, feels that way shows how universal these feelings are. 

It's A Wonderful Life, like A Straight Story, is an incredibly wholesome story, but it has a darkness underneath. Henry Potter represented both the robber barons of the past and the shift away from new deal style politics. FDR died in 1945, a year before the release of his film. His progressive VP was thrown out for Truman by the corporate DNC. About 75 years later, Sanders lost an unfair race against Clinton; the DNC was ruled by a judge to had the right to an unfair election and to select their own candidate. Time magazine estimates the average American worker would take in an extra thousand dollars a month if wealth inequality was the same as a century ago. America is Bedford Falls for some, but Pottersville for the unfortunate.

Besides saving lives in childhood, George's greatest achievement was helping all those families get homes. During the mortgage crisis, the American government didn't want to reward bad judgement by helping out those in jeopardy of losing their homes. But when it came to Wall Street they were not only too big to fail, but too big to jail. In real life, plenty of people who only care about their pleasure and their consequences get off Scott free and even get richly rewarded. Potter is like Nietzsche's blond beast with "master morality" who doesn't mind, but in fact relishes on stepping on people's dreams. George is Christ like in his generosity.

It's a masterpiece to me. But, presumably it could seem mawkish to someone who doesn't have the faith or social beliefs of a George Bailey. For a more Christmas centered movie with Jimmy Stewart, you should check out the romantic comedy A Shop Around the Corner.
A Muppet Christmas Carol is the one to watch.
I've seen It's a Wonderful Life probably twenty times minimum and it still makes me cry at several points. The heart and optimism of a Frank Capra movie is sorely missed in the modern day

> The holidays have a peak in suicides for a reason.

This is actually a myth. Suicide rates in the Northern Hemisphere are usually higher around Springtime and lower during the winter months.

Interesting. I have suicidal ideation sometimes, but I love the winter. Some people get seasonal depression. I wonder if maybe those who have year long depression are more likely to like the winter, but those with less severe depression dislike the winter.
